title: Lou Henry's offer to play the Savoy and Carney's advice
summary: Tired of Brooklyn, he took Carney's advice that the Savoy would put him on view and accepted Lou Henry's three-month job.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money

blocks.x: So we stayed there, they stayed there until around December. And I was talking to Harry Carney -- he was still rooming with me, you know. Of course, I'm down here at the beach and he...

Still in '27. Duke had been barnstorming up in New England, and they had come back; now they're getting ready to go to Philadelphia, Baltimore and Washington -- theatres there. What they call around the
world -- a show, you know. So Harry and I were talking... And after they'd finished with that, they were supposed to go into the Cotton Club.
So this fellow, Lou Henry (Lou Henry was his name, a trombone player), asked the band... What's that trumpet player's name, your boy? Anderson.

Edward Anderson was a trumpet player in the band. Lou Henry offered me the job with him; they were going in the Savoy. So I told him I'd let him know about it. He wanted it on a certain date. I was talking it over with Harry; you know, Harry Carney.

Well, I had been working out in Brooklyn all these months, so everything was all right as far as a job was concerned, or the money. But you know, I was losing my ambition. And talking to Harry, I says, "You know, Lou Henry offered me a job to go in the Savoy. What do you think of it?"

He said, "Well, I'll tell you, Charlie. You're working over in Brooklyn, and nobody sees you over there." He said, "If you go in the Savoy..." Because the job at the Savoy was only for three months. He says, "If you go in the Savoy," which was the showplace of Harlem -- anybody who comes to New York, first thing they come to is the Savoy.
All the musicians and everything else. He said, "If you go work in there, then somebody will see you. You have a better chance in New York than you have in Brooklyn."

That sounded pretty good to me. So I gave my notice then to Brooklyn, and I told Lou Henry I'd accept the job at the Savoy. So I went to work for Lou Henry at the Savoy for three months. And believe me, my stock went up just like that. Boy, people thought I was something. You'd have thought my name was in the lights down there. So...
